title: Formulating a right-tailed hypothesis test for promotional sales lift
scenario_markdown: A nationwide retail supermarket chain tests an interactive digital promotional display in its gourmet coffee aisle. Historically, stores using standard shelf placement have averaged $\mu = 50\text{ bags}$ of coffee sold per day. The merchandising VP claims that installing the digital display significantly increases average daily sales and should be rolled out chain-wide.

parameters.objective: Formulate directional right-tailed null and alternative hypotheses for sales increase

assumptions: The population parameter of interest is the long-term true mean daily unit sales mu under the digital display condition
Historical baseline without the display is established at 50 bags per day

approval.notes: Reviewed hypothesis formulation for directional claim: H0: mu <= 50 (or mu = 50) vs H1: mu > 50. Addresses common errors: swapping null and alternative, stating hypotheses about the sample statistic x_bar, and using a two-tailed formulation for a one-directional claim.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which pair of null ($H_0$) and alternative ($H_1$) hypotheses correctly states the test of the VP's claim that the digital display increases average daily sales?

options.hint_markdown: The alternative hypothesis $H_1$ always carries the research claim of an effect or increase. The null hypothesis $H_0$ maintains the status quo.
Hypotheses are always statements about unknown population parameters (such as $\mu$), never about sample statistics (such as $\bar{x}$) which are known directly from the data.
The VP's claim is explicitly directional ("increases sales"), which requires a one-tailed (right-tailed) alternative $\mu > 50$, not a two-tailed test.

stages.explanation_markdown: The claim being tested is that the display produces an increase in average daily sales above the historical baseline of $50$. In hypothesis testing, the claim to be demonstrated with empirical evidence is placed in the alternative hypothesis: $H_1: \mu > 50$. The null hypothesis represents the status quo of no increase: $H_0: \mu \le 50$ (often written simply as $H_0: \mu = 50$).

stages.prompt_markdown: In which direction does the rejection region lie, and what sample evidence would lead to rejecting $H_0$?

options.text_markdown: Right tail: $H_0$ will be rejected only if the sample mean $\bar{x}$ is substantially greater than $50$, producing a sufficiently large positive test statistic ($Z$ or $t$).
Left tail: $H_0$ will be rejected only if the sample mean $\bar{x}$ is substantially lower than $50$.
options.hint_markdown: Because $H_1: \mu > 50$, evidence in favor of the alternative lies exclusively in the upper (right) tail of the sampling distribution.

options.text_markdown: Both tails: $H_0$ will be rejected if the sample mean is either much larger or much smaller than $50$.
options.hint_markdown: A right-tailed test places the entire significance level $\alpha$ in the upper tail; an unusually low sample mean provides no evidence of a sales increase.

options.text_markdown: $H_0$ is rejected whenever $\bar{x} > 50$, regardless of the magnitude of the difference or sample size.
options.hint_markdown: A sample mean slightly above $50$ (such as $50.2$) may easily occur due to random sampling variability; rejection requires exceeding the critical value threshold.

stages.explanation_markdown: The inequality in $H_1: \mu > 50$ points to the right. Consequently, all critical area $\alpha$ is placed in the upper (right) tail. Only sample means sufficiently higher than $50$ that yield a test statistic beyond the critical value (or a $p$-value $< \alpha$) justify rejecting $H_0$ and endorsing the marketing rollout.
